title: Ibeyi - Breaking and Entering
transcript:
Lisa-Kaindé Diaz of Ibeyi spoke to Simon Winkler over Skype about Ash, the duo’s musical influences and the relationship between photography and their album artwork. Triple R dates the two-part archived interview 28 September 2017, the day before Ash was released. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: ‘River’ is from Ibeyi, the twin sisters Lisa-Kaindé and Naomi Diaz, taken from their self-titled debut album released in 2015 on XL Recordings, with production by Richard Russell. That track got them a lot of attention. Beyoncé posted a video of herself and her daughter dancing to it, and her staff reached out to Ibeyi. That led to Lisa-Kaindé and Naomi becoming involved in Lemonade, the visual album. They featured in a number of the videos, which was an incredible collaboration.

Since the release of their self-titled album they’ve been extremely busy, not least working on the follow-up Ash, which is released tomorrow, also on XL Recordings. Lauren and I have been loving the singles, particularly ‘Deathless’, which we’ve been playing quite a bit. The song is described as a rallying cry for people who feel helpless in the face of oppression. Elsewhere on the album they explore social and political issues. ‘No Man Is Big Enough For My Arms’ samples Michelle Obama’s response to obscene comments Donald Trump was recorded making in 2005. There are also quotes from Claudia Rankine’s Citizen, a book-length poem about race in America, on ‘Transmission’. I spoke with Lisa-Kaindé about the album. Although it discusses those issues, it wasn’t necessarily intended as an explicitly political album.

Lisa-Kaindé: It’s funny because when people say to us, ‘So you made a political album,’ we always say, ‘The world is making it political.’ The reason why it is political is because of what is happening around the world. We’re just talking about the way we see the world and that makes it political. But the truth is, it’s just two young women talking to women, or two young women talking about empowerment and about how important it is to feel big and to feel strong and to go for it, and how important love is. We’re just telling what we think is important and what we think we needed to share. We don’t think we have the truth. We don’t try to preach, that’s what I’m trying to say. We don’t preach, but we still try to be as truthful as we can.

I think it was important for us for that album. The first album, we talked a lot about our family and we needed to remember them with music and celebrate them with music. We needed to make an homage for them. For this album we didn’t realise, but actually we needed to talk about the world and to open it a little bit more. ‘Deathless’ was a song that we wrote, and we felt instantly a little bit more hopeful about the world just afterwards. We realised that we would get to sing and make people sing every night, ‘We are deathless.’ We would get to believe in it for three minutes, all together, the audience and ourselves. Believe in the fact that we are deathless and large and we have power and we can do things. That was so important for us.

Simon: When I was preparing for this interview, I watched a great video of both of you at Amoeba Records, talking about the different records in your bag.

Lisa-Kaindé: Oh my God, that was so long ago.

Simon: It was great to hear all the music, the jazz, soul and R&B. I think, Lisa, you mentioned hearing Nina Simone sing was like being spoken to, that all the words she sings are directed towards you. It feels very much that you and Naomi communicate in a similar way. Is that how you feel about singing and music?

Lisa-Kaindé: My God, you just compared us to Nina Simone. That is really flattering, but thank you so much. She’s our goddess, and for me she’s the number one. I’ve believed in every word she said, and she touches me in such a deep way, a deep organic way. We try to do that, actually. Thank you for saying that. We try to transmit something. That’s the whole point of what we’re trying to do. We always said it was a way to connect with our father who passed away, with ourselves, with each other. I will always say that we met each other for the first time when we started doing music together. It’s also a way to communicate with the audience. Definitely when we sing Yoruba songs every night we feel the thousands of people, millions of people, that sang those same Yoruba songs for years. We definitely feel them.

Simon: This next part of the interview looks at the duo’s interest in visual arts and the significance of photography as a source of inspiration, in particular the work of Francesca Woodman and other American artists of the early ’80s who were exploring self-portraiture as a way of expressing themselves.

Lisa-Kaindé: There’s something about photography, you feel it. It’s like music. You can see a picture and have the feeling instantly, and it can stay with you for years, months or minutes. I love that. I love the fact that once you’ve seen a photo that really impacted you, it stays with you and it lives with you. I still remember the first time I saw Francesca Woodman’s photos. It’s still in me, and it was years ago. What I love the most about her is that it’s so autobiographic. It’s so much her personality in those pictures. It’s no one else’s, it’s 100 per cent her. That’s also what I love about Frida Kahlo’s work. It’s so autobiographic. It’s so violent and visceral, but truthful, so truthful. The first album, I don’t know if you remember the cover, but it was us as babies and the same photo reproduced as us now.

Simon: That’s right, yes.

Lisa-Kaindé: That was because the last album was so much about our past. This new album is about Naomi and me mixing each other even more, and about the scars of the world, I guess. That’s how we got the idea. Also, we love blurring the identities and blurring the separation between each other. So we glued my face on Naomi’s face and Naomi’s face on my face.
